Space: China opens its station to its first foreigner, as Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali lifts off Wednesday aboard Shenzhou-24

China's manned space agency on Tuesday, November 24, presented the Shenzhou-24 crew, due to lift off Wednesday at 8:18 a.m. from Jiuquan. On board, Pakistan's Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will become the first foreign astronaut to join China's Tiangong space station, the result of an agreement signed in 2025 [1][2][3].
The launch is scheduled for Wednesday, November 25, at 8:18 a.m. Beijing time, from the Jiuquan launch center in northwestern China [1][3].

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, 40, will fly with Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, according to Xinhua, citing the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) [2]. He had been selected from two candidates put forward by Pakistan's space agency Suparco, alongside Khurram Daud [4].
It will be the first joint flight of Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program [1]. It stems from an agreement signed by China and Pakistan in February 2025 [2].
The Pakistani astronaut will be a “payload specialist,” in charge of scientific experiments. He is expected to stay about a week and return aboard Shenzhou-23 [2].
He will come back down with two Shenzhou-23 crew members at the end of their six months in orbit, Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying, Hong Kong's first astronaut [2].
The third crew member, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay six more months: it would be China's first year-long stay in orbit [2].
Key takeaway: by inviting a Pakistani astronaut, Beijing is turning its space station into a diplomatic tool and rewarding its closest ally in South Asia [1][2].

Pakistan is the first country to benefit from this opening, and it is a first for the country too: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is set to become the first Pakistani in space [3]. The symbolism matters with neighboring India, with which relations remain tense.

China is thus building an alternative to the International Space Station, run by the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Until now, only Chinese astronauts had stayed aboard Tiangong [1][4].
The Chinese program is also speeding up at home: after a first astronaut from Hong Kong, Beijing is preparing its first year-long stay in orbit [2].

Space is becoming a field of influence, just like trade. Countries that cannot send astronauts with the Americans or Europeans now have another door: Beijing's, which uses it as a selling point to get closer to countries of the Global South.

Ecuador: five days before local elections, Daniel Noboa campaigns in person for his party, which leads the polls in Quito, Guayaquil and Cuenca

Ecuadorians will elect their mayors, prefects and councilors on Sunday, November 29. There are 51,731 candidacies in the running. President Daniel Noboa is touring the country for his ADN party, which is aiming for up to 40% of local governments and leads the polls in the three largest cities [1][2][3][4].

The National Electoral Council (CNE) brought these local elections forward to Sunday, November 29, 2026 [1]. They will choose the authorities of municipalities, prefectures (provinces) and rural parish councils [3].
The election has 51,731 candidacies [3]. In Quito, ten candidates are running for mayor for 2027-2031, including incumbent mayor Pabel Muñoz and former mayor Jorge Yunda [5].

On November 23, the twelfth day of the campaign, Noboa walked the streets of Riobamba, in the Andes, alongside ADN's local candidates, list 7 [2]. He had announced he would take 7 to 15 days of leave to campaign [6].
Noboa says he is aiming for ADN officials in up to 40% of local governments [3]. He had ruled out any alliance, preferring to field his own candidates [7].

According to an AtlasIntel-Talismán poll published in mid-November, Harold Burbano (ADN) has 26.5% in Quito against 23.5% for Pabel Muñoz; in Guayaquil, Cynthia Viteri leads with 43.2% [8]. ADN candidates also lead for the prefectures of Guayas, Pichincha and Azuay [4].
Key takeaway: by taking leave to campaign alongside his candidates himself, Noboa is turning a local election into a national test of his popularity [2][6].

The ground is not won everywhere. In 2025, in the coastal province of Manabí, left-wing candidate Luisa González won 63.17% against 30.17% for Noboa [7]. The scattering of votes across many lists will be one of the decisive factors [7].
In Quito, the gap of just three points between the ADN candidate and the incumbent mayor leaves the outcome open [8]. Winning the capital would give Noboa a valuable local relay for governing.
Noboa justified the timing by the climate threat: he puts the probability of a major El Niño event, “the mother of all Niños,” at 70% [1].

Ecuador exports to Europe the bananas, shrimp and cocoa you find in supermarkets. Stable local government matters for these industries, which are often hit by insecurity and by El Niño-related bad weather.

Oil: Iran says three tankers hit mines in Hormuz, but Brent stays at a three-month low, below $89

Iran's Revolutionary Guards claim that three oil tankers caught fire on Monday, November 23, after hitting mines in the Strait of Hormuz. Yet the price of a barrel of Brent keeps falling: $88.97 on Tuesday morning, near its lowest since late August. The market now fears too much oil rather than a shortage [1][2].

According to the Revolutionary Guards navy, quoted by Iranian television channel Press TV, three oil tankers caught fire on Monday after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz. The report has not been independently confirmed [1][2].
On Tuesday morning in Asia, Brent, the global benchmark, was down 0.45% at $88.97 a barrel; US WTI fell 0.29% to $79.94 [1].
On Monday, Brent posted its lowest close since August 31, and WTI fell intraday to its lowest since August 26 [10][1].
The United States is also trying to find out whether Iran is behind cyberattacks targeting up to 50 oil tankers, according to the Wall Street Journal, cited by Reuters [1].
Traffic is slowing, though: according to data firm Kpler, about 9.5 million barrels per day passed through Hormuz over the ten days to November 19, against an average of 12.2 million in October [4].

On the supply side, Libya's Sharara pipeline has reopened. Deutsche Bank calculates that observed global inventories swelled by 52 million barrels in October, a surplus of 1.7 million barrels per day [1].
Daniel Hynes, an analyst at ANZ bank, offers a caveat: the market remains “under severe strain” despite the improvement in inventories [1][2].

Key takeaway: the oil price no longer reacts to threats, but to supply figures. Tankers on fire in Hormuz, through which 12.2 million barrels per day were still passing in October [4], would have sent prices soaring a few months ago. This time, Brent is falling [1].

For the website investingLive, this very weak reaction shows that most of the war-related “risk premium” has vanished, and that prices now follow inventory data [3]. In late April, at the height of the crisis, Brent had reached $126.41 [5]: it has lost about $37 since.

The main reason: the world once again has too much oil. Inventories are rising, Libya is pumping again, and Deutsche Bank puts the surplus at 1.7 million barrels per day [1]. But ANZ warns that the system is moving from an acute shortage to “lasting vulnerability,” not back to normal [2].
In other words, the price is low but fragile: it rests on the assumption that incidents in Hormuz stay limited. A real closure of the strait would change everything.

A barrel below $90 eventually shows up at the pump, a few weeks later, especially for diesel. But this price remains fragile: a more serious incident in Hormuz would be enough to send it back up quickly. For your heating or fuel budget this winter, the trend is rather good, with no guarantee.

How it works: the “risk premium” in the oil price

The price of a barrel depends first on supply and demand. But when a war threatens a key route like Hormuz, buyers pay extra to make sure they get their deliveries: that is the risk premium. It swells fast and falls back fast. In June 2019, after attacks on tankers in the Gulf of Oman, Brent rose as much as 4% during the day [6], before ending up about 2% [7]. During the “Tanker War” of the 1980s, the attacks did not lead to a lasting price rise, Time recalls [8]. Today, with rising inventories and a surplus estimated at 1.7 million barrels per day [1], the premium has almost disappeared [3]: a threat only pushes prices up if oil is genuinely at risk of running short.
Precedents: when tankers are attacked in the Gulf

During the US Navy's first escort, the Kuwaiti tanker Bridgeton, reflagged under the US flag, hits an Iranian mine near Farsi Island, but completes its voyage [9]. According to Time, the Tanker War neither closed Hormuz nor caused a lasting rise in oil prices [8].
Mines are spectacular, but their effect on prices stays limited when there is no shortage of oil.
Two oil tankers are attacked in the Gulf of Oman. Brent jumps as much as 4% intraday [6], from a five-month low, then ends the day up about 2% [7].
Without a real shortage, the spike fades within hours.

At the height of the Hormuz crisis, Brent hits $126.41, its highest in four years, before falling back toward $115.8 [5].
When oil is genuinely short, the risk premium explodes: the opposite of the current situation.

Seoul soars nearly 7% the day after its “Black Monday”: the Kospi climbs back above 5,000 points, triggering an upside circuit breaker

On Tuesday, November 24, the Seoul stock exchange rebounded 6.5% to 7%, depending on the source, driven by Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The Kospi climbed back above 5,000 points, from 4,708 the day before. Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia lifted AI stocks across Asia [1][5][7].
On Monday, the Kospi had fallen intraday as low as 4,586.80 points, below 4,600 for the first time in ten months, before closing at 4,708.54 [2][3].

On Tuesday, by 9:06 a.m., the index was up 268.86 points (5.71%): a buy-side “sidecar” was triggered, suspending automatic buy orders for five minutes [2]. The same mechanism kicked in on the Kosdaq, the tech-stock market [14].
It is the 29th buy-side sidecar of the year, and the 61st in total, counting both upward and downward ones [2][3].
According to AP, the Kospi gained 6.5% to 5,014.41 points, with Samsung Electronics up 7.5% and SK Hynix up 8.6% [7]. Finimize reports a 7.19% gain, to 5,047.15 points [5].
Early in the session, SK Square, SK Hynix's largest shareholder, climbed 11.47% [4].
Foreign investors returned to buy, after selling 14,790 billion won of Korean shares in November through Monday [6][1].
Elsewhere in Asia, Japan's Nikkei gained about 4%, to around 58,670 points, after a public holiday, while Hong Kong lagged behind [8].

Key takeaway: the Korean stock market has become a bet on AI chips. Samsung and SK Hynix make the memory chips Nvidia needs. When Nvidia collapses, Seoul plunges; when Nvidia jumps more than 30%, Seoul soars [1][7].
This rebound should not obscure the fall. The Kospi had hit a record close of 9,114.55 points on June 22, according to Wikipedia [13]: at about 5,000 points, it remains more than 40% below.
The number of circuit breakers also reflects market nervousness: 61 triggers since January [2]. Swings of 5% within minutes, up or down, have become almost routine.

The return of foreign investors is the signal to watch. They pulled out nearly 15,000 billion won in November [6]: if they come back for good, the rebound can hold; otherwise, it will remain a one-day bounce.

If you have an “emerging markets” or “Asia” fund, Korea carries a lot of weight in it, often with Samsung at the top. These daily swings of 5% to 7% show that these investments can move very sharply, in both directions. A spectacular rebound does not mean the decline is over.

How it works: the “sidecar,” the Seoul stock exchange's automatic brake

The Korean stock market has two brakes. The first, the sidecar, is triggered when Kospi 200 index futures move by more than 5% [10]. It then blocks orders placed by computer programs for five minutes [2], to prevent robots from amplifying the move. It works both upward and downward: on Tuesday, it was a “buy-side” sidecar that kicked in [2]. The second brake, the circuit breaker, is much rarer: it halts all trading for 20 minutes when the index falls more than 8%, as on August 5, 2024 [9]. These pauses do not change the market's direction, but give investors time to think.
Precedents: the Seoul stock exchange's big jolts

In the midst of the Covid panic, the Kospi jumps 8.6% [10] and climbs back above 1,600 points; a buy-side sidecar is triggered during the session [11].

The Korean stock market amplifies fears coming from the United States.

In 2026, giant swings have become frequent in Seoul, both up and down.

news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.tit: Paris climbs back above 8,000 points and the French state borrows slightly more cheaply: the CAC 40 gains 1.5%, STMicroelectronics jumps 9%
news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.sum: On Monday, November 23, the CAC 40 gained 1.48% to 8,044.84 points, ending five sessions of losses. AI-related stocks, led by STMicroelectronics (+8.96%), drove the rise. Meanwhile, the French state's ten-year borrowing rate eased to around 4.83% [1][3][5].
news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.poi: The CAC 40 rose 117.09 points (+1.48%) to 8,044.84 points, after a 1.89% drop on Friday to 7,927.75 points [1].
The Paris index thus ended a run of five consecutive declines [3]. It is back above 8,000 points [2].
Chipmaker STMicroelectronics led the gains: +8.96% to €40.01. Legrand gained 4.20% to €132.75, and Schneider Electric 4.11% to €235.85 [1][4].
Conversely, Orange lost 1.55% to €14.88 and Carrefour 0.22% to €13.47 [1].
The trigger came from the United States: Jensen Huang's return to the helm of Nvidia sent the stock up more than 30% and pulled European markets along [4][10].
The yield on the ten-year OAT, the rate at which the French state borrows, fell to 4.833%, from 4.875% in the previous session and 4.937% on November 19 [5]. Agence France Trésor shows 4.83% [6].
“The news on the Nvidia side is sweeping away everything else, the reaction is very strong,” sums up an analyst quoted by Boursorama [1].
news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.why: Key takeaway: the Paris stock exchange now depends heavily on Wall Street's mood about AI. STMicroelectronics, Legrand and Schneider Electric, which supply chips, electrical hardware and equipment for data centers, accounted for most of the rise [1][4].
Defensive stocks, such as Orange or Carrefour, fell [1]: when investors regain confidence, they sell safe-haven shares to buy back riskier stocks.

The quiet good news comes from the bond market. In late October, France's ten-year rate had exceeded 5% [7][8]. It has come back to 4.83% [5][6]. Every tenth of a point counts: it is the price at which the state finances its debt, and it serves as a benchmark for household and business loans.
This one-day rebound does not erase everything: as recently as November 17, the CAC 40 stood at 8,216 points [9]. The market remains hanging on the next news from Nvidia and AI.
news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.for: If you have a PEA (French stock savings plan) or unit-linked life insurance, this rebound recovers some of last week's losses, not all of them. The drop in the state's borrowing rate matters more to you in the medium term: if it lasts, it can slow the rise in mortgage rates.

news.2026-11-24-paris-cac40-8000-oat.dee: How it works: the state's borrowing rate and the stock market

The French state finances its deficit by selling bonds, called OATs. Their ten-year yield is the price investors demand to lend to it. When they buy more OATs, their price rises and their yield falls: that is what happened on Monday, with the rate moving from 4.875% to 4.833% [5]. A lower rate helps the stock market in two ways. It reduces the cost of credit for companies. And it makes shares more attractive by comparison: when a risk-free bond pays less, investors are more willing to accept the risk of shares. Conversely, in late October, when the French rate exceeded 5% [7], worries about public debt weighed on the markets.

Cooling AI data centers: Switzerland's ABB buys Germany's Ziehl-Abegg for $2.65 billion, and its shares rise

Swiss industrial group ABB announced on Monday, November 23, the acquisition of Ziehl-Abegg, a family-owned German maker of fans and motors, for an enterprise value of $2.65 billion. The goal: to benefit from the boom in data centers, which need cooling. ABB shares gained more than 2% [1][2][5].
ABB is paying an enterprise value of $2.65 billion, including debt, or $2.22 billion for the shares, according to its press release cited by Evertiq [2].
Ziehl-Abegg makes energy-efficient fans, electric motors and ventilation systems for air conditioning, data centers and elevators. It is expected to post about $1.4 billion in revenue in 2026 [2].
The family-owned, unlisted company employs about 6,300 people in Europe, the Americas and Asia. ABB promises to keep its headquarters in Künzelsau, in Baden-Württemberg [3][4].
Data centers accounted for about 9% of ABB's revenue in 2025: it is its fastest-growing business [1].
ABB CEO Morten Wierod says he sees no slowdown in data center investment, despite recent market nervousness about AI [1].

ABB shares gained 1.3% right after the announcement [6], 2.1% according to Reuters, and more than 5% intraday, up to 68.66 Swiss francs [5]. They had lost 26.7% since their record of 89.14 francs in June [4].
Completion is expected in the second half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval [1][2].
Key takeaway: AI does not just sell chips. Servers get extremely hot, and fans, motors and cooling systems are needed to keep them running. ABB is buying a specialist in this equipment [1][3].

It is also a contrarian bet. The acquisition comes in the middle of a correction in AI stocks, but ABB considers demand solid [1]. Analysts at Zurich Cantonal Bank consider the deal consistent with ABB's acquisition history [4].

The acquisition is part of a race for cooling specialists: in 2025, US group Eaton had already bought Boyd Thermal [8][9]. ABB wants to bring its new subsidiary's margin up to the level of its Motion division within three years [2].

For Germany, it is another jewel of the Mittelstand, the family-owned industrial companies, passing under foreign control. The promise to keep the headquarters in Künzelsau therefore matters a lot [3].

If you hold a European equity fund, ABB and Schneider Electric are often part of it: these groups benefit from the AI boom without making chips. It is a less risky way, though not risk-free, to be exposed to this theme. For jobs in Europe, keeping the German headquarters is good news.

How it works: enterprise value and share price

In an acquisition, two prices circulate. Equity value is what the buyer pays the owners: here $2.22 billion [2]. Enterprise value adds the debt the buyer takes on: here $2.65 billion [2]. The difference, about $430 million, therefore mostly corresponds to Ziehl-Abegg's net debt. To compare acquisitions, analysts divide enterprise value by revenue or by earnings. Eaton paid $9.5 billion for Boyd Thermal, or 22.5 times its expected 2026 operating profit [8], for $1.7 billion in sales [9]. ABB is paying less than 2 times sales for Ziehl-Abegg [2]: a company less specialized in liquid cooling, but also cheaper.
Precedents: the race for cooling specialists
October 2024
France's Schneider Electric buys 75% of US company Motivair, a specialist in liquid cooling for data centers, for $850 million in cash [7].
Europe's electrical giants started buying cooling building blocks early.
October 8, 2025
ABB sells its robotics division to Japan's SoftBank for $5.375 billion, instead of listing it on the stock market. The business accounted for $2.3 billion in sales, about 7% of the group [10][11].
ABB is refocusing on electrification and motors: Ziehl-Abegg fits this strategy.
November 3, 2025
US group Eaton buys Boyd Thermal for $9.5 billion, or 22.5 times its expected 2026 operating profit; $1.5 billion of its $1.7 billion in sales comes from liquid cooling [8][9].
Cooling for AI comes at a very high price: ABB is buying cheaper, but less specialized.
